survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PIRLS 2016 ePIRLS 2016 international assessment microdata (67,070 students across 15 countries/regions) to evaluate operationally feasible automatic scoring of constructed-response text. The manuscript describes item- and country/language-specific training and evaluation (including 5-fold cross-validation repeated five times) and multilevel modeling of linguistic variance, but it does not report applying PIRLS sampling weights or any replicate-weight procedure. Because the automatic scoring models (XLM-R embeddings with SVM; fuzzy lexical matching) are trained and evaluated as ML classifiers/matchers and the paper does not mention survey-weighted estimation, the analysis is treated as unweighted. The only explicit data preparation steps described are exclusions of blank responses with invalid human scores, exclusion of responses without captured human scores, and recoding of misclassified valid responses to 0 for consistency in accuracy/QWK computations.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: This project report does not analyze PV-based cognitive achievement outcomes. The dependent variables are (a) automatic scoring agreement/accuracy metrics against human item scores for constructed-response text, and (b) linguistic variance measures (STTR) derived from sets of text responses; these are not PV-based achievement scores generated by PIRLS. Missingness is handled through explicit exclusions/recoding rules for blank responses and for responses without captured human scores, but the manuscript does not describe a general missing-data imputation strategy for other variables, so a missing-data handling category is not fully specified.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The analytic dataset covers 67,070 students from 15 countries/regions who participated in PIRLS 2016 ePIRLS using 14 test languages. The analysis of constructed-response items includes 51 CR items, excluding one CR item that only involved ordering of numbers, yielding 50 items. For scoring-model training/evaluation, blank text responses were excluded when humans assigned scores other than the intended code 9 (blank responses scored as 0, 1, 2, or 3; total n=1,693+1,934+188+2=3,817 responses, 0.3% of all responses). Responses with no captured human score were excluded. Additionally, non-empty valid text responses misclassified as 9 were recoded to 0 (incorrect) to preserve linguistic variance while affecting QWK due to weighting.

main_findings.dataset_used: PIRLS 2016 ePIRLS (2016) constructed-response text scoring across 15 countries/regions
main_findings.target_variable: Automatic scoring accuracy (XLM-R; quadratic weighted kappa)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Average agreement: κ = .755 across all items and country-language groups (5-fold CV repeated five times). Linguistic variance STTR correlated negatively with accuracy: Pearson r = −.235; Spearman ρ = −.314 (p < .001). Multilevel model: STTR coefficient negative (Table 5, Model 2/3): Estimate −.267*** (SE .027) and −.111*** (SE .022) after controlling for item characteristics.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PIRLS 2016 ePIRLS constructed-response text scoring the study leveraged linguistic variance (STTR) together with item characteristics (cognitive process, item difficulty, maximum points, and item position) to predict automatic scoring accuracy for the XLM-R+SVM semantic classifier, finding that higher linguistic variance was significantly associated with lower accuracy (average κ ≈ .755; STTR negatively related to κ with r ≈ −.235). This indicates that these patterns have implications for educational policy and instructional practice, though cross-sectional ILSA designs cannot establish causality.

main_findings.dataset_used: PIRLS 2016 ePIRLS (2016) constructed-response text scoring across 15 countries/regions
main_findings.target_variable: Automatic scoring efficiency (FLM; proportion of responses scored automatically)
main_findings.performance_metrics: FLM efficiency (automatic scoring coverage) ranged from 17.1% to 37.9% with median 26.1% across language-country groups. Linguistic variance STTR correlated negatively with FLM efficiency: Pearson r = −.393; Spearman ρ = −.230 (p < .001). Multilevel model: STTR coefficient negative (Table 6, Model 2/3): Estimate −.769*** (SE .041) and −.626*** (SE .060) and reduced to −.626*** after controlling for item characteristics (Model 3 shows smaller magnitude).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PIRLS 2016 ePIRLS constructed-response text scoring the study leveraged linguistic variance (STTR) and item characteristics to predict fuzzy lexical matching (FLM) efficiency, finding that higher linguistic variance significantly reduced the share of responses that could be scored automatically (median efficiency ≈ 26.1%; STTR negatively related to efficiency with r ≈ −.393). This indicates that these patterns have implications for educational policy and instructional practice, though cross-sectional ILSA designs cannot establish causality.

main_findings.dataset_used: PIRLS 2016 ePIRLS (2016) constructed-response text scoring across 15 countries/regions
main_findings.target_variable: Automatic scoring accuracy (FLM; exact agreement / QWK)
main_findings.performance_metrics: FLM produced a grand mean accuracy of .971 (Table 7). Linguistic variance did not significantly impact FLM accuracy: STTR coefficient not significant in Model 2 (Estimate −.026, SE .017) and not significant in Model 3 (Estimate .032, SE .023).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PIRLS 2016 ePIRLS constructed-response text scoring the study leveraged linguistic variance (STTR) and item characteristics to predict FLM accuracy, finding that linguistic variance did not significantly affect FLM accuracy (grand mean accuracy ≈ .971; STTR effects were non-significant), consistent with FLM’s score-propagation design that already conditions on response similarity. This indicates that these patterns have implications for educational policy and instructional practice, though cross-sectional ILSA designs cannot establish causality.

main_findings.dataset_used: PIRLS 2016 ePIRLS (2016) constructed-response text scoring across 15 countries/regions
main_findings.target_variable: Linguistic variance decomposition (STTR) explained by item and student characteristics
main_findings.performance_metrics: Two-level model ICC for language-country groups: ρ = .199 (M1). Item characteristics explained 50.1% of item-level STTR (marginal R² = .501; Table 3). Three-level model: student characteristics explained 27.1% of linguistic variance (marginal R² = .271; Table 4, M3), and the most general model explained 51.1% of fixed-effect variance (marginal R² = .511; Table 4, M4) with conditional R² up to .837 and total explained variance up to 83.7% when including random effects.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PIRLS 2016 ePIRLS constructed-response text the study leveraged item characteristics (cognitive process, passage, item position, maximum points, and item difficulty) and student characteristics (gender and L1/L2 status) to explain linguistic variance measured by STTR, finding that item-related factors accounted for a large share of STTR variability (marginal R² ≈ .501 at item level) and that higher linguistic variance was associated with lower automatic scoring performance. This indicates that these patterns have implications for educational policy and instructional practice, though cross-sectional ILSA designs cannot establish causality.

data.outcome_summary: This project report evaluates operationally feasible automatic scoring of 2016 ePIRLS constructed-response text using two approaches: fuzzy lexical matching (FLM) and a semantics-based supervised classifier using XLM-R embeddings with SVM. Across 50 CR items and 15 countries/regions, XLM-R achieved an average human-machine agreement of κ = .755 (5-fold CV repeated five times), while FLM achieved a high grand mean accuracy of .971 but only scored about 26.1% of responses automatically on average (median), with efficiency ranging roughly 17.1%–37.9%. Linguistic variance operationalized via STTR showed a significant negative relationship with XLM-R accuracy (Pearson r = −.235; Spearman ρ = −.314) and with FLM efficiency (Pearson r = −.393; Spearman ρ = −.230), whereas STTR did not significantly affect FLM accuracy. Multilevel analyses further showed that item characteristics (process, passage, position, maximum points, difficulty) explained substantial portions of STTR variability (e.g., marginal R² ≈ .501 for item-level STTR). The study does not report survey-weighted estimation and uses human scores as the gold standard, with noted human misclassification noise that may affect training and evaluation.
